title: What Is the Lord's Supper?
excerpt: Christians agree that Jesus gave his church a meal of bread and wine and commanded it to be kept, and they have disagreed for five hundred years about what he meant by four words spoken over the bread.
body:
A visitor at a wedding watches the congregation file forward and is told, kindly, that this part is not for her. A man kneels at a rail with his hands open and believes that what is laid in them is the body of the Lord who made him. In another building a tray of small cups passes down the row in silence, and a boy of ten holds his very still because his mother has told him what it stands for. And a skeptic who came for a friend's baptism hears a minister say "this is my body" over a loaf of bread and wonders what on earth he has walked into.

His question is the right one. The first outsiders who heard reports of the meal assembled them into a rumor of cannibalism. The skeptic today is more likely to notice something else, and it is harder to answer. Christians call this the meal of their unity. It is also the place where they most visibly part. A Christian may be welcome to sing, pray and give in a church of another tradition and then be asked to stay in the pew when the bread comes. A faith whose family meal has a guest list like that, the skeptic says, doesn't believe its own words about one body.

Most of that is true, and the reasons for it are older and more serious than they look from the pew.

## The Night It Was Given

The meal began inside another meal. Jesus had come to Jerusalem for the Passover, the supper at which Israel remembered the night God brought the nation out of Egypt. The law called that day "a memorial day" to be kept "throughout your generations" (Exodus 12:14), and every household told the story again as though it had been there. "I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer," Jesus told the twelve (Luke 22:15).

Then he did something no host at that table had done. "Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, 'Take, eat; this is my body.' And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, 'Drink of it, all of you, for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins'" (Matthew 26:26–28). Luke adds the command: "Do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19).

Paul handed on the same words to the church at Corinth, and added what the meal says each time it is kept: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes" (1 Corinthians 11:26). Earlier in the letter he had put it as a question: "The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?" (1 Corinthians 10:16).

Those few sentences are nearly everything the New Testament says about the Supper, and every tradition is reading the same ones. The whole disagreement is over what Jesus meant by "is," what Paul meant by "participation," and what it is to do something "in remembrance."

One more passage is always on the table. In John 6, well before that night, Jesus told a crowd in Galilee, "Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life" (John 6:54), and many of his followers left over it. A few lines later he said, "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all" (John 6:63). Some Christians hear the Supper in the first sentence. Others hear in the second a warning against reading it that way.

## What the First Christians Left Us

The earliest writings outside the New Testament show the meal at the center of Christian life, and they don't settle the later argument.

The *Didache*, a church manual usually dated around the year 100, gives a prayer over the broken bread: "Even as this broken bread was scattered over the hills, and was gathered together and became one, so let Thy Church be gathered together from the ends of the earth into Thy kingdom." It is a prayer of thanks, and it says nothing about what the bread becomes. Around the year 110 Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to be killed in Rome, wrote of people who denied that Christ had a real body, and said they stay away from the meal "because they confess not the Eucharist to be the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ." Around 150 Justin explained the meal to a pagan emperor: "For not as common bread and common drink do we receive these."

Christians who believe Christ's body is present in the bread hear their own faith in Ignatius and Justin. Christians who hold the meal as a remembrance point out that neither man explains how he means it, that both speak the way Jesus spoke, and that the *Didache* speaks another way. For centuries the church kept the meal and issued no definition of how Christ is present in it. The definitions came later, when people began to press the question.

## Five Answers

There are five main answers, and each has documents of its own to speak for it.

The Roman Catholic Church teaches that the bread and wine become Christ. The Council of Trent stated it in 1551. After the consecration, "our Lord Jesus Christ, true God and man, is truly, really, and substantially contained under the species of those sensible things." The look, taste and weight of bread remain, and what the thing is has changed: "a conversion is made of the whole substance of the bread into the substance of the body of Christ our Lord," a change the Church "suitably and properly" calls transubstantiation. The word had been in official use since a council of 1215. For Catholics the meal is also a sacrifice. It does not add a second sacrifice to the cross. It is the one sacrifice made present: "the victim is one and the same," the council said in 1562, "the manner alone of offering being different." The governing conviction is that Jesus said "is," and that the Lord who made the world by speaking can do what his words say.

The Eastern Orthodox churches confess the same change and decline to explain it. John of Damascus, whose eighth-century summary of the faith the Orthodox still honor, wrote that "the bread itself and the wine are changed into God's body and blood." Then he stopped. "But if you enquire how this happens, it is enough for you to learn that it was through the Holy Spirit." The manner, he said, "cannot be searched out." The Orthodox call the meal the holy mysteries.

Lutherans confess a real presence without a change of substance. Luther's *Small Catechism* of 1529 asks what the sacrament is and answers, "It is the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, under the bread and wine, for us Christians to eat and to drink, instituted by Christ Himself." The bread is still bread, and the body of Christ is truly given with it. The Lutheran confession of 1530 says the body and blood "are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat." What Lutherans guard is the gift. If Christ's presence depended on the strength of the believer's faith, the meal would be emptiest when a person needed it most, so the catechism points away from the believer to two words: "the words 'For you' require nothing but believing hearts."

The Reformed churches teach a real feeding on Christ by the Spirit. The bread and wine are not changed, and Christ's risen body is in heaven. Yet the meal is no empty sign. The Westminster Confession says that worthy receivers "do then also inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified." The Heidelberg Catechism of 1563 has the believer say that as surely as the bread and cup are tasted, "so surely does He Himself nourish and refresh my soul to everlasting life with His crucified body and shed blood." The Church of England's Articles speak the same way: the body of Christ is received "only after an heavenly and spiritual manner." The conviction here is that the Holy Spirit joins believers on earth to a Christ who has truly ascended, and that a body which is everywhere at once would no longer be a human body.

The memorial view holds that the Supper is a remembrance, a proclamation and a pledge. Huldrych Zwingli, the reformer of Zurich, wrote in 1523 that the mass "is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us." A Baptist confession of 1858 says the Supper "is in no sense a sacrifice, but is designed to commemorate His death, to confirm the faith and other graces of Christians, and to be a bond, pledge and renewal of their communion with Him, and of their church fellowship." Those who hold this view refuse the word mere. The Passover was a memorial, and at that table each generation of Israel was to see itself brought out of Egypt. The site's study of the sacraments has the memorialist say that the bread carries "the weight a wedding ring carries, which is not nothing." The conviction is that Christ's sacrifice was finished once, that he named the purpose of the meal himself when he said "in remembrance of me," and that the church has a long record of ending up adoring bread.

The lines between these are less tidy than a list suggests. The Baptist confession written in London in 1677 says believers "spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified," in words taken nearly whole from Westminster.

## The Hard Question for Each

Every one of the five has a text it finds difficult, and its best teachers admit it.

The memorial view has to reckon with the word "is," and with Paul's word "participation." It also has to account for his warning that a person can become "guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 11:27), which is strong language for mishandling a symbol. The traditions of presence have to reckon with "in remembrance" and "you proclaim," which are the purposes the text itself states, and with the plain fact that Jesus was sitting at the table in his body when he said the bread was his body. The Catholic account is asked whether a philosophy of substance, drawn from Aristotle, should be binding on a fisherman's meal. The Lutheran is asked how a human body can be in ten thousand places. The Reformed is asked by both sides whether a spiritual feeding by faith finally differs from devout remembering. The Orthodox are asked whether refusing to explain is an answer.

None of those questions is foolish, and none has made the other side go away in five hundred years.

## Marburg

In October 1529 the two leading reformers, Luther and Zwingli, met at Marburg. A Protestant prince, the Landgrave Philip, had arranged the meeting to bring the two sides together. They parted without agreeing on the Supper.

The site's history course says of that day that Protestantism learned there "the skill it has practiced ever since: dividing over real differences among those who agree on almost everything, and calling the division faithfulness." We should feel the weight of that sentence, because both men were right that the question mattered and both feared God. And we have kept doing what they did.

## Who May Come

The question of the guest list is as old as the meal. The *Didache* says, "let no one eat or drink of your Thanksgiving (Eucharist), but they who have been baptized into the name of the Lord." Justin gives three conditions: the person believes what the church teaches, has been baptized, and "is so living as Christ has enjoined." From the start the table was for the baptized, and it was never a meal for whoever happened to be passing.

Paul's warning stands behind every later rule. "Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself" (1 Corinthians 11:28–29). Corinth explains the warning. The church met in homes, and the wealthy were eating their own fine food while poorer members went without. "One goes hungry, another gets drunk" (1 Corinthians 11:21). The sin Paul names is contempt for the brother at the same table. Some read "the body" he tells them to discern as Christ's body in the bread, and others as the congregation itself. Either way, a meal meant to proclaim the Lord's death had become a display of rank.

The churches have drawn the line in different places, and each has a reason that deserves to be heard as its holders give it. The Catholic Church gives communion to Catholics, and Trent asks that no one "conscious to himself of mortal sin" come without first confessing it. Many Lutheran and Reformed churches guard the table; the Heidelberg Catechism invites those "who are truly displeased with themselves because of their sins and yet trust that these are forgiven them." Many Baptist churches have held, in the words of the 1858 confession, that baptism "is prerequisite to church fellowship, and to participation in the Lord's Supper," and since they understand baptism as the immersion of a believer, the line follows from that.

If you have been asked to stay in the pew, it may help to know what was usually meant. In most cases the church was not saying that you are no Christian. It was saying that the meal means more to it than hospitality, and that it won't pretend to a unity that hasn't been reached.

## What We Have Done With It

The church's failures at this table should be said plainly. We have fought over it. In the century after Marburg Christians burned, drowned and made war on one another, and what this meal is was among the questions a person could be condemned for answering wrongly. We have made it small: in many congregations the meal is occasional, hurried, an appendix to the service, kept by people who could not say what they believe happens in it. We have made it a wall and felt no grief about the wall. And in churches of every tradition we have done what Corinth did, eating beside people whose need we never noticed.

Paul's rebuke to Corinth was that their divisions made the meal something other than what Jesus gave: "When you come together, it is not the Lord's supper that you eat" (1 Corinthians 11:20). No tradition should assume that sentence is about someone else.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess together that Jesus gave this meal on the night he was betrayed and commanded his church to keep it, that it proclaims his death for sinners, that he is the host, and that it looks ahead to a feast still to come. The creeds say nothing about how he is present in it.

How he is present, and who may come, are questions of the second order. They are serious, because a congregation has to do one thing or another every time it gathers. They have divided churches for five centuries without dividing the faith, and people on every side of them confess the same Lord. This essay has set the five answers side by side and does not choose among them.

At the first Supper Jesus knew who was at the table. One of the twelve had already agreed to sell him, another would deny him before morning, and the rest would run. He knew it when he broke the bread, and after the cup he said it aloud: "the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table" (Luke 22:21). Then he made a promise that is still open. "I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom" (Matthew 26:29).

He is still waiting to drink it. Every divided table on earth is set in the meantime, by people who can't yet eat together, in memory of a Lord who intends that one day they will.

*"Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread."* (1 Corinthians 10:17)

*"For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes."* (1 Corinthians 11:26)
